title: Faithful and modest
hook: you help your city not by holding office but by being trustworthy and self-respecting (Enchiridion 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday: keep your footing, enstasis, your stance. Your line was keep my footing. Did you skip one automatic yes and say something honest and kind? Day three hundred fifty-six.

Down the hall lives the neighbor who signs for your packages and actually remembers to tell you. Who returns the ladder. Who says she'll water the plants while you're away, and you come home to plants that are alive. She doesn't sit on the city council. She'll never have a plaque. But the whole building runs a little better because she's in it. Section twenty-four of the handbook imagines a student who worries that a philosopher with no money and no office is useless to his friends and his city. Epictetus answers him, and that neighbor is in the answer. Today: faithful and modest.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR WHO SIGNS FOR PACKAGES.` → `NO OFFICE, NO PLAQUE.` → `IS A PHILOSOPHER USELESS?`

segments.voice: First, the worry. Don't let thoughts like this trouble you, Epictetus says: I'll live without honor, a nobody everywhere. Getting an office, being invited to a dinner, those aren't up to you. So how can missing them be your dishonor? You only need to be somebody in what's yours, and there you can be worth a great deal. Second, the friends. But my friends will get no help from me, the student says. What help? Epictetus asks. Money? Roman citizenship? Who told you those were in your power? Show me how to get them while staying trustworthy and self-respecting and generous, and I'll get them. But if you ask me to lose my own good so you can have things that aren't truly good, see how unfair that is. And what would you rather have, he asks: money, or a faithful, self-respecting friend? Third, the city. But my country will get no help from me. What help? It won't get colonnades or public baths from you. Fine. It doesn't get shoes from the blacksmith either, or weapons from the shoemaker. It's enough if each does their own work. If you made one more citizen trustworthy and self-respecting, would that be no use? Fourth, the two words. Faithful is pistos: trustworthy, the one whose word holds. Modest is aidemon: self-respecting, with a sense of shame in the good sense, the person who won't do what's beneath them. What place will you hold in the city, then? Whatever place you can hold while staying faithful and modest. Lose those trying to help, he says, and what use will you be, faithless and shameless? The neighbor with the ladder already knows this.
screen: `A NOBODY EVERYWHERE?` · `MONEY, OR A FAITHFUL FRIEND?` · `NO BATHS FROM YOU, AND THAT'S FINE.` · `PISTOS AND AIDEMON.` · then, large: `FAITHFUL AND MODEST.`

segments.voice: Think of one small promise you've made lately that's still open. Returning something. Answering a message. Showing up when you said. Picture the person waiting on it. Picture yourself keeping it today, simply, without fuss. Notice how small it is, and how much it says. Then let the words settle in you, slowly, with the breath: faithful, on the in breath; modest, on the out. The bell holds the time.
Pistos. The Greek word for faithful, trustworthy, the one whose word holds; Epictetus' answer to feeling useless: you already serve your friends and your city. Today's word.
Your line: each does their own work. Be reliable in one small thing today: keep the little promise you pictured, and don't mention it. Day three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners measure their usefulness less by status or money than by being trustworthy and self-respecting in ordinary dealings.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 24: faithful and modest, trustworthy and self-respecting.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble and loyal.
what it means: you serve friends and city best by being trustworthy and self-respecting, not by office or money.
what a scholar hears: aidemon carries aidos, the Greek sense of shame or reverence that holds a person back from what's beneath them.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): replaced the sweeping 'every apartment building has one' opener; the worried student is now framed as the chapter's imagined questioner rather than a claim about real students; 'the party' became 'a dinner' to match the text; softened the trapdoor's root claim.

Greek πιστὸς καὶ αἰδήμων in Enchiridion 24 (in the accusative in the text): confirm.
